keep: The idea is named in one line up front (a vector is a size with a direction) with Khan's quote on exactly those words, and scalars are set against it with a case from his work: a pump's mass is a scalar, its weight a vector.

The picture is the brief's arrow that slides: dragging the middle moves the arrow while the readout holds at 3 across, 4 up, size 5, which shows the cause (a vector is only its size and direction) and answers the moved-vector misconception, with Bitesize's 'regardless of their position' on the words it supports.
One worked example with numbers computed from the rule: |a| = √(3² + 4²) = 5, 2a = 6 across and 8 up, size 10, the unit vector 0.6 across and 0.8 up.

Twelve screens alternating SHOW (1, 3, 5, 7, 9) and DO (2, 4, 6, 8, 10), ending with mixed puzzles (11, 12). Each misconception the brief names for lesson 1 has a puzzle with its own wrong picks: scalar against vector (step 2, the pump; step 11, the boat), a moved arrow as a new vector (step 4, four arrows), AB against BA (step 6) and a negative number reversing (step 8), plus dividing by the moves added for a unit vector (step 10).
The course puzzle is touched once, without teaching adding: 10 + 10 + 4 = 24 A is the size-only sum the LibreTexts quote rules out.
fix: Causal step skipped: the size is said to come 'by Pythagoras' without why. Say the across and up moves are at right angles, so the arrow is the long side of a right-angled triangle.

Causal step skipped: '2a runs 6 across and 8 up' states the rule without the reason. Build it from what he can picture: 2a is a done twice, so each move doubles, the triangle grows in proportion and the direction holds.
False absolute: 'Every multiple of a lies along the same line, so they are all parallel' includes 0a, which has no direction. Name the arrows a, 2a and −2a instead.
Shape: five paragraphs where the prompt allows two to four; the course-puzzle sentence sits in its own paragraph. Fold it into the end of the third.
BA = −AB is stated straight after AB with no picture of why. Add that going from B back to A covers the same ground the other way.
The unit vector is named but not shown to hold the direction alone; say so, so the practice's 'heading with the speed taken out' has its ground.

Analogy too thin and its 'breaks' carries a false absolute ('always a distance'). Give the scaled step (three saddles on, 900 mm across and 1,200 mm up) so it reproduces scaling as well as sliding, and say honestly where it breaks: a vector can be a force or velocity, and a real force's point of action matters for turning though the vector does not hold it.
Practice's mistakes list misses the speed-against-velocity slip that step 11 catches. Add it, so the dossier carries every misconception the screens catch.

faults.interactive shows only the effect: no: the slide shows the cause, a readout that holds while the position changes
faults.checks test recall: not applicable in read mode; the puzzles ask him to apply the rule to new arrows
faults.thin or decorative research: no: all five sources are cited on words their quotes support
faults.unreadable labels: no: readouts say across, up and size in words

shape: Idea in one line up front, the rule in words, one worked example computed from the rule, the misconceptions shown failing in the puzzles and practice, a trade analogy with its break, practice with steps, a rule of thumb, a worked example and the mistakes, and a bold recap he could say back.
